Port Jackson shark (Heterodontus portusjacksoni) neonates emerge from their encapsulated eggs at a fork length of approximately 20 cm [Lb = approximately 20 cm], a size that allows them to begin foraging on hard-shelled benthic invertebrates almost immediately following yolk-sac resorption. This comparatively large birth size, which reflects an extended period of yolk-dependent embryonic development, provides a survival advantage against the diverse array of predators that patrol the temperate reef systems of southern Australia. Field surveys conducted across multiple nursery bays in New South Wales have consistently recorded pups measuring within a narrow range around this value, suggesting relatively canalized birth dimensions that may be linked to the constraints imposed by the large, spirally-fluted egg case. The onset of exogenous feeding in these juvenile individuals marks a critical transition, with young sharks subsisting primarily on small crustaceans before their jaw musculature becomes sufficiently developed to process larger prey items such as sea urchins and gastropods. Growth proceeds steadily during the first year, though mortality remains high as these immature individuals must balance the competing demands of predator avoidance and energy acquisition.

At a stable water temperature of 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C], the period between oviposition and hatching spans approximately 365 days [ab = approximately 365 days], one of the longest incubation durations recorded among elasmobranch species of comparable body size. This remarkably protracted embryonic phase is closely tied to the relatively cool thermal regime of the temperate coastal waters where this species deposits its eggs, and it stands in stark contrast to the faster developmental rates seen in tropical heterodontids. During this year-long incubation, the developing embryo relies entirely on its substantial yolk reserves, progressing through successive organogenesis stages until it attains the size necessary to emerge as a fully formed, miniature replica of the adult. The temperature dependency of this process has been experimentally verified, with eggs maintained at higher temperatures exhibiting accelerated development at the cost of reduced hatchling size. Comparisons with congeneric species suggest that the lengthy incubation period of Port Jackson shark may represent an adaptation to seasonally variable food availability, ensuring that pups emerge during periods of peak prey abundance.

First reproduction in female Port Jackson sharks has been documented to occur at approximately 12.5 years after birth [tR = approximately 12.5 years after birth], although a secondary estimate from a different study places this milestone at roughly 9 years after birth [tR = roughly 9 years after birth] when both assessments were conducted under the same thermal conditions of 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C]. This discrepancy between the two reported ages at first reproduction likely reflects geographic variation in growth rates or differences in the criteria used to define reproductive readiness across distinct populations. Both values, however, underscore the comparatively slow life-history pace of this species relative to many other coastal sharks, a pattern that emerges from its low metabolic demand and the consistent, moderately cool environment it inhabits. Following the onset of reproductive activity, females alternate between periods of foraging and egg-laying, typically depositing their distinctive auger-shaped egg cases in rocky crevices that offer protection from egg predators. The delayed maturation of this species carries significant implications for its population dynamics, as only a fraction of any given cohort will survive to contribute reproductively.

The ultimate fork length attained by adult Heterodontus portusjacksoni in the wild has been estimated at approximately 151 cm [Li = approximately 151 cm], based on back-calculation from vertebral growth band counts in mature individuals. This asymptotic size, which corresponds to the theoretical maximum body length that the species can achieve, is approached progressively as growth increments diminish with advancing age. Growth curve analyses converged on an asymptotic fork length of about 151 cm [Li = about 151 cm], an estimate that proved robust across two independent modeling frameworks applied to the same vertebral dataset. Among the largest specimens examined during extensive long-term field studies, total lengths exceeding 160 cm have been recorded, though these outliers are notably rare and typically represent exceptionally old individuals. The conversion from total length to fork length, which the original growth analyses employed to standardize measurements across variable tail morphologies, accounts for the slightly compressed fork-length values relative to total length. This maximum body size is consistent with the general allometric patterns observed across the Heterodontiformes order and reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a diet consisting predominantly of hard-shelled benthic prey.

Sexual maturity in Port Jackson shark, defined by the functional development of claspers in males and the onset of ovarian follicular growth in females, occurs at a fork length of approximately 67.4 cm [Lp = approximately 67.4 cm], with a separate analysis from a different population indicating a puberty fork length of about 60 cm [Lp = about 60 cm]. These length-at-maturity estimates, spanning roughly 60 to 67 cm fork length, correspond to a total length range of approximately 64 to 83 cm in adult females and underscore the substantial proportion of ultimate body size that individuals must attain before reproductive activation begins. The gonadal recrudescence that accompanies this size threshold is mediated by endocrine signals linked to body condition and energy reserves, ensuring that only healthy individuals invest in the costly process of egg production. Following puberty, adult females typically produce between 10 and 16 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 10 and 16 eggs per clutch], and field evidence indicates they commonly deposit approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year] at 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C]. This moderate annual reproductive output is offset by the species' substantial longevity; the maximum recorded lifespan reaches approximately 33 years [am = approximately 33 years], a remarkable duration that allows for numerous repeated breeding seasons over the course of an individual's lifetime at a temperature of 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C].
